questions.question: What is the Boolean derivative (Boolean difference) of predicate p with respect to clause c, denoted pc?

options.A: pc = p(c=true) ⊕ p(c=false)

questions.explanation: The Boolean difference pc is formally defined as p(c=true) XOR p(c=false). It evaluates to true if and only if changing c changes the value of p.

questions.question: What does pc = true indicate regarding clause c and predicate p?

options.A: Clause c determines predicate p under those minor clause truth assignments.
options.B: Clause c has no effect on predicate p.

questions.explanation: When pc evaluates to true, the truth value of p depends directly on c; toggling c will toggle p. Hence c determines p.

questions.question: For predicate p = a ∧ (b ∨ c), what is the condition for clause 'a' to determine p, computed via pa?

options.A: b ∨ c must be TRUE.

questions.explanation: pa = p(a=T) ⊕ p(a=F) = (T ∧ (b ∨ c)) ⊕ (F ∧ (b ∨ c)) = (b ∨ c) ⊕ F = b ∨ c. Thus, 'a' determines p whenever (b ∨ c) is TRUE.

questions.question: For predicate p = a ∨ (b ∧ c), what is the condition for clause 'a' to determine p?

options.A: ¬(b ∧ c) must be TRUE (i.e. at least one of b or c is FALSE).
options.C: b must be TRUE and c must be TRUE.
options.D: b and c must both be TRUE.

questions.explanation: pa = p(a=T) ⊕ p(a=F) = (T ∨ (b ∧ c)) ⊕ (F ∨ (b ∧ c)) = T ⊕ (b ∧ c) = ¬(b ∧ c). Thus 'a' determines p when b ∧ c is FALSE.

questions.question: What algebraic identity applies when simplifying XOR expressions with FALSE: X ⊕ FALSE?

options.A: X

questions.explanation: In Boolean algebra, XOR with false is the identity operation: X ⊕ 0 = X.

questions.question: What algebraic identity applies when simplifying XOR expressions with TRUE: X ⊕ TRUE?

options.A: ¬X

questions.explanation: XOR with true inverts the value: X ⊕ 1 = ¬X (NOT X).

questions.question: For predicate p = a ⊕ b, what is pa (the condition under which clause 'a' determines p)?

options.A: TRUE (clause 'a' ALWAYS determines p, regardless of b!)

questions.explanation: pa = (T ⊕ b) ⊕ (F ⊕ b) = ¬b ⊕ b = TRUE. In an XOR predicate, any clause always determines the predicate regardless of the other clause's value!

questions.question: If pc simplifies to FALSE for some clause c, what does this imply about clause c in predicate p?

options.A: Clause c is redundant (irrelevant) and can never determine predicate p under any condition.
options.B: Clause c is the most important clause.
options.D: Clause c must be tested 100 times.

questions.explanation: If pc = FALSE, no truth assignment to minor clauses can ever allow c to toggle p. Clause c is logically dead/redundant in that predicate.

questions.question: How can Karnaugh maps (K-maps) or truth tables assist in finding ACC test cases?

options.A: By finding adjacent cells in the map differing in only clause c where the output cell values differ (one 1, one 0).
options.C: By converting Boolean logic into assembly code.
options.D: By proving the code has no memory leaks.

questions.explanation: In a K-map, adjacent cells differ by exactly one variable (clause). If two adjacent cells along variable c have opposite outputs (one 1, one 0), they form an exact RACC test pair for c.

questions.question: What is an 'infeasible test requirement' in logic coverage?

options.A: A clause assignment that violates semantic constraints (e.g. requiring x > 5 to be true AND x < 2 to be true simultaneously).
options.B: A test that takes more than 1 millisecond.
options.D: A test requirement with no ID.

questions.explanation: Clauses are not always independent; relational expressions sharing variables may be contradictory (e.g., x < 0 and x > 10 cannot both be true), making certain rows of the truth table infeasible.

questions.question: If a clause assignment is infeasible, what is the proper action in RACC/CACC testing?

options.A: Recognize the constraint, declare the requirement infeasible, and select an alternate feasible test pair (or document the infeasibility).

questions.explanation: Infeasible test requirements cannot be satisfied by any real execution input; they must be identified, documented, and excluded from achievable coverage goals.

questions.question: For predicate p = (a ∧ b) ∨ (a ∧ c), what is pa?

options.A: b ∨ c

questions.explanation: Factoring gives p = a ∧ (b ∨ c). When a=T, p = b ∨ c. When a=F, p = F. pa = (b ∨ c) ⊕ F = b ∨ c.

questions.question: When can RACC be impossible to satisfy while CACC is satisfiable?

options.A: When clause dependencies or multiple occurrences of a clause prevent minor clauses from remaining identical while toggling p.
options.B: Never; RACC and CACC are identical.
options.D: Only when predicates contain no variables.

questions.explanation: If a clause appears multiple times in different parts of an expression or has relational dependencies, fixing minor clauses identically might be impossible, while allowing correlated variations (CACC) succeeds.

questions.question: In the predicate p = a ∧ b, which pair of (a, b) inputs satisfies RACC for major clause a?

options.A: (T, T) and (F, T)

questions.explanation: For major clause a, minor clause b must be fixed to T. The test pair is (a=T, b=T) [p=T] and (a=F, b=T) [p=F].

questions.question: In the predicate p = a ∨ b, which pair of (a, b) inputs satisfies RACC for major clause a?

options.A: (T, F) and (F, F)

questions.explanation: For major clause a, minor clause b must be fixed to F. The test pair is (a=T, b=F) [p=T] and (a=F, b=F) [p=F].

questions.question: Can the test (T, T) for p = a ∧ b be reused as the 'c is true' test when testing major clause b under RACC?

options.A: Yes! For b=T with a=T, the test is (T, T). This enables sharing test cases across clauses to minimize test suite size.
options.C: Only if b is defined as a global variable.

questions.explanation: For clause a, tests are (T, T) and (F, T). For clause b, tests are (T, T) and (T, F). The test (T, T) is shared, giving a total of only 3 tests: {(T, T), (F, T), (T, F)} for N+1 = 3 tests.

questions.question: What is the boolean difference for p = ¬a with respect to clause a?

options.A: pa = ¬T ⊕ ¬F = F ⊕ T = TRUE

questions.explanation: Inverting a single clause always determines its negation: changing a from T to F changes ¬a from F to T. The derivative is identically TRUE.

questions.question: What algorithmic representation allows efficient computation of boolean derivatives for large predicates?

options.A: Binary Decision Diagrams (BDDs)

questions.explanation: Reduced Ordered Binary Decision Diagrams (ROBDDs) provide canonical representations of Boolean functions, enabling fast Boolean difference and satisfiability checks.

questions.question: Suppose p = a ↔ b (equivalence / XNOR). What is pa?

options.A: TRUE (toggling a always changes whether a equals b)

questions.explanation: a ↔ b is the negation of XOR (a XNOR b). Like XOR, toggling either operand unconditionally flips the equivalence, so pa = TRUE.

questions.question: What is the primary practical goal of logic coverage algorithms in safety-critical software engineering?

options.A: To systematically prove that each decision condition independently controls program branching without requiring exhaustive 2^N testing.
options.B: To eliminate the need for functional specifications.
options.C: To automatically translate code into assembly.

questions.explanation: Logic coverage algorithms (like RACC/MC-DC) mathematically ensure that every single decision clause is tested to show it can independently affect execution, achieving near-exhaustive confidence with linear test effort.
